analysis.one_liner: Lifts the federal ban on offshore natural gas drilling and shares royalties with coastal states and energy programs.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 171 cosponsors but never received a committee markup or floor vote, and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the long-standing federal moratorium that keeps most of the Outer Continental Shelf — federal waters off U.S. coasts — closed to natural gas leasing, while leaving the ban on offshore oil leasing in place. It sets up a buffer: no gas leases within 25 miles of a coast, state approval required within 50 miles, and states could veto leases between 50 and 100 miles out, though a disapproval law would lapse after two years unless renewed. Money from new leases would be split between the Treasury, drilling-adjacent states, and dedicated funds for environmental restoration, renewable energy research, and home energy aid for low-income households.
analysis.who_benefits: Offshore natural gas drillers gain access to vast federal waters that are currently closed to leasing. Coastal states with new production would receive 37.5% of bonus bids and royalties for uses including education, transportation, and tax reduction. Low-income households would benefit from a dedicated 2.5% royalty stream for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) and the Weatherization Assistance program, and regional restoration funds (Chesapeake Bay, Great Lakes, Everglades, and others) would receive fixed shares of royalties.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gas drillers, coastal states, low-income energy users

how_it_helps.text: Dedicates a fixed 2.5% of new lease bonus bids and royalties to LIHEAP home energy aid and the Weatherization Assistance program, both of which help low-income households heat and weatherproof their homes.

Splits another 32% of royalties into dedicated reserve accounts for energy efficiency and renewables research, carbon capture and sequestration, and restoration of the Chesapeake Bay, Great Lakes, Everglades, Colorado River Basin, and San Francisco Bay.
Pays producing states 37.5% of bonus bids and royalties, usable for education, transportation, tax reduction, coastal restoration, and disaster insurance programs.
Expresses Congress's intent that expanded offshore gas development support American manufacturing and good jobs, and states the goal of affordable energy from the Outer Continental Shelf.

analysis.who_pays: Coastal communities and ocean users would bear the environmental risk of new offshore gas development in waters now closed to leasing, including risks to fisheries and coastal tourism. The federal Treasury would give up the majority of new lease revenues — more than 65% of each dollar goes to states and reserve accounts rather than the general fund. Offshore drilling carries inherent risks of spills and disturbance, and the bill's state-veto design is asymmetric: a state's approval of leasing can never be repealed, while its disapproval expires after two years unless the state re-enacts it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coastal communities and the federal Treasury

drawbacks.text: The bill would open nearly the entire Outer Continental Shelf to gas leasing by voiding all presidential and statutory withdrawals of submerged lands, ending a protection that has kept these waters closed to drilling.

Its state-veto mechanism is lopsided: a state law approving leases has permanent effect and cannot be undone by repeal, while a law disapproving leases between 50 and 100 miles offshore expires after two years unless the state acts again to extend it.
Only 25% of new lease revenues would go to the general fund; 37.5% goes to producing states and 37.5% to reserve accounts, reducing federal revenue relative to current law.

New leases would allow production of natural gas 'and associated condensate,' and lessees who discover oil deposits during exploration would follow regulations the Interior Secretary writes — raising the prospect of oil development under nominally gas-only leases while the offshore oil moratorium formally remains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill packages an industry priority — access to closed federal waters — with real public benefits: dedicated funding for home energy aid, restoration projects, and state revenue sharing. But the core of the bill is terminating the offshore leasing moratorium, and its design leans toward more drilling: state vetoes are weaker than state approvals, and the buffer zones are modest. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the environmental risk to coastal waters falls on the public and on coastal industries, while the certainty of new lease access goes to gas drillers, with the royalty carve-outs serving partly as the political price of opening those waters.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2007, referred to three committees and then a Natural Resources subcommittee, and sat there without a markup or floor vote until the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. John Peterson (R-PA) introduced the bill on June 20, 2007, joined by original cosponsors including Reps. Neil Abercrombie (D-HI), Thelma Drake (R-VA), Devin Nunes (R-CA), Chet Edwards (D-TX), and Charlie Melancon (D-LA).
It was referred to the Natural Resources, Rules, and Budget Committees on the day of introduction.
On June 29, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources of the Natural Resources Committee; no further committee action is recorded.
The bill amassed 171 cosponsors — 152 Republicans and 19 Democrats — but never received a committee markup or a vote in either chamber before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without any vote, the status quo won: the offshore natural gas moratorium stayed in place, coastal waters were not opened to leasing, and the gas industry gained nothing from this bill. Supporters of the bill also gained nothing — no royalties flowed to energy assistance or restoration funds under it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal-protection status quo; drillers gained nothing

for.name: Rep. John Peterson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor in November 2007.

for.name: 19 of 202 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors from gas-producing and coastal states.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral; Chair Nick Rahall (D-WV)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, which never reported it; no markup was ever scheduled and the bill never reached the floor.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not schedule the bill for floor consideration; majority Democrats broadly supported retaining the offshore drilling moratorium during this period.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Republican — 152 of 171 cosponsors — with 19 Democrats, and the bill received no action in the Democratically controlled committees.

industries.note: The bill's core purpose is to open the entire Outer Continental Shelf to gas leasing, creating a major new business opportunity for offshore gas drillers on federal lands now closed to them. Consumers could see more domestic gas supply, and part of the royalties would fund home energy aid, but the industry would gain access to a public resource while coastal communities bear the environmental risk.

New gas drilling within 25–100 miles of state coastlines would introduce industrial activity into waters that currently host tourism and commercial fishing. These industries' interest in keeping waters undisturbed runs alongside the public's interest in protecting coastlines.

The bill dedicates 2.5% of new lease revenues to LIHEAP and the Weatherization Assistance program, creating a new funding stream tied to drilling activity — funding that depends on the industry's leases being issued.

The bill leaves the offshore oil moratorium untouched, but gas-only leases would allow production of associated condensate and let existing lessees convert to gas-restricted development, partially opening the oil-and-gas lease system to reformulated activity.
